The exact current marker is INTERVIEW-61-91264fb93a1067e6. The screen asks for solve(a,b) to return the minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions, and replacements transforming a into b, with no stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Use dynamic programming: D(i,j) is the minimum cost to transform the first i characters of a into the first j characters of b. Initialize D(0,j)=j and D(i,0)=i. Each remaining entry is the minimum of D(i−1,j)+1 for deletion, D(i,j−1)+1 for insertion, and D(i−1,j−1) plus zero for matching characters or one for replacement. These cover the possible final operations, so the minimum is optimal.

With one rolling row, the invariant before updating column j is that dp[j] holds the previous row’s value, dp[j−1] holds the current row’s left value, and a saved diagonal holds D(i−1,j−1). After updating, dp[j] equals D(i,j); save the old dp[j] for the next diagonal.

Boundary cases: two empty strings return zero; one empty string returns the other’s length; identical strings return zero. Using the shorter string for columns gives O(min(a.length,b.length)+1) extra space and O(a.length × b.length) cell updates. Swapping the strings preserves the distance because insertion and deletion have equal costs. No implementation yet.

Invariant: after processing i digits, the current count equals the number of valid decodings of exactly that prefix. Keep only the two preceding counts, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Internally, use one way to decode the empty prefix to seed the recurrence, but explicitly return zero for empty input as required.

Boundary cases: a leading zero returns zero; an internal zero must belong to 10 or 20. Thus "10" returns 1, "30" and "100" return 0, and "226" returns 3. The attachment does not specify a maximum length or how counts exceeding JavaScript’s safe-integer range should be represented.

Use dynamic programming: let dp[i] be the minimum cost to reach position i before paying there. Starting at index 0 or 1 is free, so dp[0]=dp[1]=0. For i≥2, dp[i]=min(dp[i−1]+cost[i−1], dp[i−2]+cost[i−2]); return dp[cost.length], treating that position as the top.

Invariant: before computing position i, the two stored values are the optimal costs to reach i−2 and i−1. Every route into i comes from one of those positions and pays that departure stair, so taking the minimum covers both possibilities. Only two previous values are needed: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

Boundary cases: two stairs give min(cost[0],cost[1]); zero-cost stairs need no special handling. The attachment gives no minimum array length or cost bounds. Under the usual nonnegative-cost interpretation, empty and single-element arrays return 0; negative costs would require revisiting the starting-state initialization, so that assumption should be confirmed.
